name: [Switch] switch-core has stopped reporting
message:
No metrics have arrived from switch-core for 15 minutes.

This is a no-data alert, and it cannot tell you which of three things happened: the server is down, it cannot reach the collector, or someone turned reporting off. Check the pod first — if it is serving, the other two are the ones left.

Note that every other monitor in this set goes quiet at the same time, so treat this one as the reason the rest went silent rather than as an outage on its own.

name: [Switch] the database is unreachable
message:
switch-core's readiness check cannot reach the database.

This is the one dependency that takes the server out of service, so Kubernetes has already emptied the Service — and because switch-core runs as a single replica there is nothing else serving. Every request is failing.

Check the database before the pod: the pod is reporting the fault, not causing it.

@REPLACE-WITH-NOTIFICATION-HANDLE

name: [Switch] no room messages are being delivered
message:
The Postgres LISTEN connection that wakes every room's delivery is down.

The API still answers and rooms still accept writes, so from outside Switch looks healthy — and no message reaches anybody. That combination is why this is alerted separately from the database check.

It reconnects itself with backoff, which is why it does not fail readiness: restarting the pod would drop every live session without fixing it any faster. Ten minutes of this means the backoff is not winning.

name: [Switch] a collaboration bridge has crashed
message:
A configured collaboration bridge is no longer running.

The platform it serves is cut off — messages from that Slack, Mattermost, Discord, Teams or Telegram channel reach nobody, and nothing Switch sends reaches it. The rest of Switch is unaffected, deliberately: a dead adapter must not take the whole server off the air.

A bridge that crashes removes itself and does not retry, so this needs a restart of that bridge rather than waiting.

name: [Switch] messages are being dropped on delivery
message:
The delivery loop has failed to deliver {{value}} time(s) in ten minutes.

Each one is a message written to a room that a client never received. The loop swallows these on purpose so one bad room cannot stop the others, so nothing else will surface them — the counter is the only evidence.

The logs carry the room and the client for each: search for "Delivery failed for client".

@REPLACE-WITH-NOTIFICATION-HANDLE

name: [Switch] the event loop is stalling
message:
A fixed-interval task is waking more than a second late.

switch-core is single-threaded and cooperative, so this is not one slow thing — it is everything at once. Room delivery, bridge dispatch and agent heartbeats are all waiting on the same loop, and heartbeats arriving late make live agent connections look lapsed through no fault of their own.

A synchronous call on the event loop is the usual cause. The stall itself is the bug; whatever timed out because of it is a symptom.

@REPLACE-WITH-NOTIFICATION-HANDLE

name: [Switch] the database pool is nearly exhausted
message:
More than 90% of the connection pool has been checked out for ten minutes.

What happens next is that requests start waiting for a connection rather than failing, so the symptom is latency everywhere and then a readiness check that times out — which reads as "the database is down" when the database is fine and this server is holding all of it.

Look for a query holding a connection longer than it should before raising the pool size.

name: [Switch] server errors are elevated
[Switch] a bridge is failing to relay
message:
{{platform.name}} has failed {{value}} time(s) {{direction.name}} in fifteen minutes.

Inbound failures are messages a person sent that nobody received; from the platform's side that is indistinguishable from being ignored. Outbound failures are Switch's replies not arriving.

The bridge is still running — a crashed one is a different alert. This is usually the platform rate-limiting, an expired token, or a channel the app was removed from.
